analysis.one_liner: Bans organophosphate and neonicotinoid pesticides and paraquat, and lets citizens petition to ban other dangerous pesticides.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 5 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would immediately cancel federal approval of three classes of pesticides: organophosphates (linked to brain damage in children), neonicotinoids (linked to pollinator decline), and paraquat (linked to Parkinson's disease and organ failure). It would also let ordinary people petition to have other pesticides declared dangerous, force the EPA to act on those petitions within 90 days or have the pesticide deemed dangerous automatically, and suspend any pesticide already banned in the European Union or Canada pending a fast review. It adds protections for farmworkers, including bilingual labels, mandatory reporting of pesticide poisonings, and protection against retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits: Children exposed to neurotoxic residues, farmworkers who handle pesticides daily, rural communities near sprayed fields, pollinators and the food supply that depends on them, and organic farmers who compete against pesticide-intensive operations. Ordinary consumers gain from fuller disclosure of inert ingredients, which can make up 99 percent of a product and include toxic chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmworkers, children, rural communities, and pollinators

how_it_helps.text: Immediately and permanently cancels the registration of all organophosphate pesticides, all seven named neonicotinoids, and paraquat, with no further proceedings, and bans continued sale of existing stocks [S2][S3].
Lets any interested person petition to designate a pesticide as dangerous; the EPA must respond within 90 days, and if it fails to do so the pesticide is deemed dangerous by default [S3].

Immediately suspends any pesticide registered in the U.S. that the European Union or Canada has banned, pending an expedited review in which the EPA may not weigh the economic cost of the ban [S2][S3].
Caps conditional registrations at two years and cancels outstanding ones not yet fulfilled, ending a practice the bill notes covered nearly 65 percent of EPA pesticide registrations [S2][S3].
Requires full disclosure of inert ingredients on labels, which the bill's findings note can account for 99 percent of a product and include carcinogenic and toxic chemicals [S3].

Requires pesticide labels in English and Spanish, creates mandatory employer reporting of farmworker poisonings with fines and criminal penalties for failure to report or retaliate, offers $25,000 rewards for reporting unreported incidents, and shields reporting farmworkers from immigration action [S3].
Lets local communities enact their own pesticide restrictions where states currently block them, and lets any person sue the EPA in federal court to enforce the law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers lose approval for major product lines overnight. Farmers who currently depend on organophosphates, neonicotinoids, or paraquat lose access to those tools and would need substitutes, which in some crops may cost more or work less well. These costs would show up partly in food production costs.

drawbacks.text: The cancellations take effect immediately with no case-by-case scientific or economic review, and the bill bars the EPA from weighing costs when reviewing foreign bans, which could remove chemicals some U.S. farmers have few ready substitutes for and raise production costs [S3].

An EU or Canadian ban would be enough to suspend a pesticide here pending review, importing other countries' risk judgments, which critics argue may reflect conditions or evidence not applicable to U.S. use [S3].

Farmers and the agriculture committee's jurisdiction means real-world transition costs for commodity crops would fall partly on growers and consumers, an honest supporter would concede the immediate-deactivation design trades certainty for speed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health protections are substantial and targeted at exposures with strong scientific support, particularly for farmworkers and children, and the automatic-deadline design exists because the EPA has let review of long-approved pesticides drag on for years. The costs are real but concentrated: the agrochemical industry loses flagship products and some growers face a forced transition. The design choice to skip case-by-case economic review makes the bill stronger for health and weaker for predictability in agriculture.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on November 30, 2021, with Sens. Gillibrand, Sanders, Warren, and Padilla as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no committee vote, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers kept their registrations for organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, and the status quo on conditional registrations, emergency exemptions, and undisclosed inert ingredients remained in place. Farmworkers and communities exposed to these chemicals gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat and overhaul pesticide review.

for.name: 4 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Gillibrand, Warren, Padilla, and Sanders among them)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Agrochemical manufacturers
against.role: Pesticide industry (makers of paraquat and neonicotinoids)
against.what_they_did: Opposed bills of this kind and lobbied against restrictions on their flagship products, and no Agriculture Committee action followed.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat, so the split was within the majority party rather than between parties.

industries.note: The bill would immediately cancel approval of organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, core commercial products, and would let citizen petitions plus foreign bans pull other products off the market. Their financial interest lay in keeping these chemicals registered, which ran directly against the health protections ordinary people would have gotten.

Growers relying on the banned chemicals would lose established tools and face transition costs, though reduced exposure also protects farmworkers and rural residents who are part of the same communities.
Producers already operating without these chemicals would face less drift and residue contamination and a more level market as competitors' tools are restricted.
